result.abstract: The lecture describes the brainstem, the stalk connecting the cerebrum to the spinal cord and cerebellum, made of the midbrain, pons and medulla oblongata. It covers its embryological origin, external and internal configuration, where each cranial nerve emerges, the fourth ventricle, the reticular formation and the tracts running through it. It ends with the blood supply from the basilar artery, the vital functions of the brainstem and the alternating syndrome.

concepts.name: Brainstem
concepts.definition: The stalk connecting the cerebrum to the spinal cord and cerebellum, lying in the posterior cranial fossa on the clivus. It has three parts from above down (midbrain, pons, medulla), gives rise to ten of the twelve cranial nerves and runs vital functions.

evidence.quote: The brainstem connects the cerebrum to the spinal cord and cerebellum.
The brainstem is the structure that connects the cerebrum to the spinal cord and cerebellum.

concepts.name: Midbrain
concepts.definition: The uppermost and smallest part of the brainstem, about 2 cm long, passing through the tentorial opening (foramen of Pacchioni). It has two parts: the tectum behind the cerebral aqueduct and the paired cerebral peduncles anterolaterally.

evidence.quote: Midbrain: smallest, 2 cm; tectum with four colliculi; peduncles with CN III between them.
The midbrain is the smallest of the three regions of the brainstem, measuring around 2cm in length.

concepts.name: Pons
concepts.definition: The middle and largest part of the brainstem. Its ventral bulge, about 2.5 cm, is made by transverse pontocerebellar fibres, and the basilar groove in its ventral midline holds the basilar artery.

evidence.quote: Its ventral bulge, about 2.5 cm, is made by transverse pontocerebellar fibres.
Pons: largest; basilar artery in the basilar groove; CN V to VIII.

concepts.name: Medulla oblongata
concepts.definition: The lowest part of the brainstem, continuous below with the spinal cord. Its ventral surface bears the pyramids and olives, and it houses the respiratory and cardiovascular centres.

evidence.quote: Medulla: pyramids (corticospinal), olives (inferior olivary nucleus)
the respiratory and cardiovascular centres are in the medulla

concepts.name: Thalamus
concepts.definition: A structure belonging to the diencephalon; it is not part of the brainstem.

evidence.quote: The thalamus is NOT brainstem.
The thalamus belongs to the diencephalon.

concepts.name: Posterior cranial fossa
concepts.definition: The cranial fossa in which the brainstem lies, resting on the clivus under the tentorium cerebelli.

evidence.quote: It lies in the posterior cranial fossa, on the clivus, under the tentorium cerebelli
Brainstem: midbrain, pons, medulla, in the posterior cranial fossa on the clivus.

concepts.name: Mesencephalon
concepts.definition: The third embryonic vesicle, which forms the midbrain.

evidence.quote: Midbrain | Mesencephalon (third vesicle)
the mesencephalon (third vesicle)

concepts.name: Metencephalon
concepts.definition: The fourth embryonic vesicle, which forms the pons together with the cerebellum.

evidence.quote: Pons | Metencephalon (fourth vesicle)
The largest part, from the metencephalon with the cerebellum.

concepts.name: Myelencephalon
concepts.definition: The fifth embryonic vesicle, which forms the medulla oblongata.

evidence.quote: Medulla oblongata | Myelencephalon (fifth vesicle)
the myelencephalon (fifth vesicle)

concepts.name: Cerebellar peduncle
concepts.definition: One of three paired peduncles (superior, middle and inferior) by which each part of the brainstem is connected to the cerebellum behind it. The peduncles also form part of the side walls of the fourth ventricle.

evidence.quote: Behind, the cerebellum by the cerebellar peduncles: superior to the midbrain, middle to the pons, inferior to the medulla.
Each part of brainstem is connected to cerebellum by cerebellar peduncles (superior, middle & inferior).

concepts.name: Superior cerebellar peduncle
concepts.definition: The cerebellar peduncle that connects the midbrain with the cerebellum.

evidence.quote: Cerebellar peduncles: superior to midbrain, middle to pons, inferior to medulla.
Superior peduncle connects midbrain with cerebellum

concepts.name: Middle cerebellar peduncle
concepts.definition: The cerebellar peduncle that connects the pons with the cerebellum; the largest of the three.

evidence.quote: middle → pons (largest)
Middle peduncle connects pons with cerebellum

concepts.name: Inferior cerebellar peduncle
concepts.definition: The cerebellar peduncle that connects the medulla oblongata with the cerebellum.

evidence.quote: Cerebellar peduncles: superior to midbrain, middle to pons, inferior to medulla.
Inferior peduncle connects medulla oblongata with cerebellum

concepts.name: Tectum
concepts.definition: The part of the midbrain behind the cerebral aqueduct. It houses four rounded colliculi, two superior and two inferior, just below the pineal gland.

evidence.quote: Tectum, behind the cerebral aqueduct: two superior and two inferior colliculi below the pineal gland.
The tectum houses four rounded prominences named colliculi which sit directly inferior to the pineal gland.

concepts.name: Superior colliculus
concepts.definition: One of the upper pair of rounded prominences of the tectum on the back of the midbrain, linked with the retina by the superior brachium and concerned with vision.

evidence.quote: The superior brachium links the superior colliculus with the retina (vision)
The upper pair of bumps on the back of the midbrain: visual reflexes.

concepts.name: Inferior colliculus
concepts.definition: One of the lower pair of rounded prominences of the tectum on the back of the midbrain. Its fibres, with those of the lateral lemniscus, run in the inferior brachium to the medial geniculate body (hearing).

evidence.quote: the inferior brachium carries lateral lemniscus and inferior colliculus fibres to the medial geniculate body (hearing)
The lower pair of bumps on the back of the midbrain: auditory pathway.

concepts.name: Superior quadrigeminal brachium
concepts.definition: A band extending laterally from the superior colliculus that forms a pathway between the superior colliculus and the retina of the eye, serving vision.

evidence.quote: The superior brachium links the superior colliculus with the retina (vision)
Superior quadrigeminal brachium forms a pathway between the superior colliculus and the retina of the eye( vision).

concepts.name: Cerebral peduncle
concepts.definition: One of the paired pillars on the anterolateral midbrain, running from the cerebral hemispheres to converge at the pons and carrying descending fibres. The two are separated anteriorly in the midline by the interpeduncular fossa.

evidence.quote: Cerebral peduncles, paired and anterolateral, separated by the interpeduncular fossa.
The paired cerebral peduncles extend from the cerebral hemispheres to converge as they meet the pons.

concepts.name: Cerebral aqueduct
concepts.definition: The part of the ependymal cavity of the brainstem that runs through the midbrain, with the tectum lying behind it.

evidence.quote: Aqueduct runs through the midbrain.
Tectum: located posterior to the cerebral aqueduct

concepts.name: Oculomotor nerve
concepts.definition: Cranial nerve III, which emerges from the anterior surface of the midbrain between the two cerebral peduncles, in the interpeduncular fossa.

evidence.quote: Anterior, midbrain | III between the cerebral peduncles
The oculomotor nerve (CN III) is seen exiting from between the peduncles

concepts.name: Trochlear nerve
concepts.definition: Cranial nerve IV, which emerges from the dorsal surface of the midbrain below the inferior colliculi before sweeping round to the anterior surface. It is the only cranial nerve that emerges dorsally.

evidence.quote: Posterior, midbrain | IV, the only nerve emerging dorsally
Inferior to the colliculi, the trochlear nerve (CN IV) emerges before sweeping across to the anterior surface.

concepts.name: Trigeminal nerve
concepts.definition: Cranial nerve V, a large nerve that emerges from the lateral aspect of the mid-pons.

evidence.quote: CN V, trigeminal | Lateral mid-pons
Cranial nerve V: trigeminal originates from the lateral aspect of mid pons

concepts.name: Abducens nerve
concepts.definition: Cranial nerve VI, which emerges at the pontomedullary junction close to the midline, the most medial of the nerves in the bulbopontine groove.

evidence.quote: CN VI, abducens | Pontomedullary junction, near the midline
Cranial nerve VI: abducens originates from the pontomedullary junction, close to the midline

concepts.name: Facial nerve
concepts.definition: Cranial nerve VII, which emerges at the cerebellopontine angle, the more lateral aspect of the pontomedullary junction, with the intermediate nerve of Wrisberg (VII bis) and the vestibulocochlear nerve lateral to it. Its fibres loop round the abducens nucleus.

evidence.quote: CN VII, facial | Cerebellopontine angle
Cranial nerve VII: facial originates from the cerebellopontine angle, the more lateral aspect of the pontomedullary junction.

concepts.name: Vestibulocochlear nerve
concepts.definition: Cranial nerve VIII, which emerges lateral to the facial nerve at the cerebellopontine angle.

evidence.quote: CN VIII, vestibulocochlear | Lateral to CN VII
Cranial nerve VIII: vestibulocochlear originates laterally to the facial nerve.

concepts.name: Glossopharyngeal nerve
concepts.definition: Cranial nerve IX, one of the mixed nerves, which leaves the lateral surface of the medulla behind the olive, above the vagus.

evidence.quote: Lateral, behind the olive | IX, X and XI, the mixed nerves
Glossopharyngeal nerve (IX): leaves the medulla behind the olive, above the vagus.

concepts.name: Vagus nerve
concepts.definition: Cranial nerve X, one of the mixed nerves, which leaves the lateral surface of the medulla behind the olive, below the glossopharyngeal nerve.

evidence.quote: Lateral, behind the olive | IX, X and XI, the mixed nerves
Vagus nerve (X): leaves the medulla behind the olive, below IX.

concepts.name: Accessory nerve
concepts.definition: Cranial nerve XI, one of the mixed nerves; its cranial part emerges from the sulcus behind the olive of the medulla, below the glossopharyngeal and vagus nerves.

evidence.quote: Lateral, behind the olive | IX, X and XI, the mixed nerves
CN IX, X and the cranial part of XI, from above downwards, from the sulcus behind the olive

concepts.name: Hypoglossal nerve
concepts.definition: Cranial nerve XII, which emerges from the anterior surface of the medulla in the sulcus between the pyramid and the olive.

evidence.quote: CN XII emerges between pyramid and olive
Hypoglossal(12th): from sulcus between pyramid & olive

concepts.name: Optic nerve
concepts.definition: Cranial nerve II, running from the eye to the optic chiasm; with the olfactory nerve, one of the two cranial nerves that do not arise from the brainstem.

evidence.quote: All cranial nerves arise from the brainstem except the optic and olfactory nerves.
runs from the eye to the optic chiasm

concepts.name: Olfactory nerve
concepts.definition: Cranial nerve I; with the optic nerve, one of the two cranial nerves that do not arise from the brainstem.

evidence.quote: All cranial nerves arise from the brainstem except the optic and olfactory nerves.
All cranial nerves arise from the brainstem, with the exception of two: the optic nerve and the olfactory nerve.

concepts.name: Basilar artery
concepts.definition: The artery lying in the basilar groove on the midline of the ventral surface of the pons. With its branches it gives the vascular supply of the brainstem.

evidence.quote: The basilar groove holds the basilar artery.
The brainstem receives vascular supply from the basilar artery and its branches.

concepts.name: Pontomedullary junction
concepts.definition: The landmark defined by the angle between the lower border of the pons and the upper border of the medulla. Cranial nerves VI, VII and VIII emerge there from medial to lateral, and the fourth ventricle is widest at its level.

evidence.quote: VI, VII, VIII at the pontomedullary junction (medial to lateral)
The pontomedullary junction is an important anatomical landmark defined by the angle between the lower border of the pons and the superior border of the medulla.

concepts.name: Cerebellopontine angle
concepts.definition: The angle at the junction of the pons, medulla and cerebellum, where the cerebellar flocculus, the choroid plexus and the emerging cranial nerves VII and VIII surround the foramen of Luschka, the lateral aperture of the fourth ventricle.

evidence.quote: The cerebellopontine angle, where CN VII and VIII emerge beside the foramen of Luschka, lies at the junction of pons, medulla and cerebellum.
The angle formed at the junction of the pons, medulla, and cerebellum is another anatomical landmark and is named cerebellopontine angle.

concepts.name: Facial colliculus
concepts.definition: A bulge in the floor of the fourth ventricle, on the posterior surface of the pons, formed by the fibres of the facial nerve looping round the abducens nucleus.

evidence.quote: Facial colliculus: facial fibres looping around the abducens nucleus.
The facial colliculus is a bulging formed by the fibres of the facial nerve looping around the abducens nucleus.

concepts.name: Stria medullaris of the fourth ventricle
concepts.definition: A bundle of nerve fibres crossing the floor of the fourth ventricle transversely from the lateral aspect into the midline. It marks the posterior border between the pons and the medulla.

evidence.quote: the stria medullaris marking the pons-medulla border
The stria medullaris of the fourth ventricle is a bundle of nerve fibres crossing transversely from the lateral aspect into the midline.

concepts.name: Fourth ventricle
concepts.definition: The ependymal cavity behind the pons and medulla. Its roof is the superior and inferior medullary vela, its floor the rhomboid fossa and its side walls the vela and cerebellar peduncles; CSF leaves by the median foramen of Magendie and two lateral foramina of Luschka.

evidence.quote: Roof: the superior and inferior medullary vela. Floor: the rhomboid fossa. Side walls: the vela and cerebellar peduncles.
CSF exits via Magendie (median) and Luschka (lateral)

concepts.name: Rhomboid fossa
concepts.definition: The diamond-shaped depression on the dorsal surface of the pons and the upper half of the medulla that forms the floor of the fourth ventricle.

evidence.quote: fourth ventricle floor is the rhomboid fossa
The floor, located ventrally, is formed by the rhomboid fossa, a diamond-shaped depression on the dorsal surface of the pons and upper half of the medulla.

concepts.name: Obex
concepts.definition: The most caudal tip of the fourth ventricle.

evidence.quote: obex at its caudal tip
The obex is the most caudal tip of the fourth ventricle.

concepts.name: Fastigium
concepts.definition: The peak of the fourth ventricle, within the cerebellum, lying under the fastigial nucleus.

evidence.quote: The peak is the fastigium; the caudal tip the obex
The peak of the fourth ventricle within the cerebellum is the fastigium and it underlies the fastigial nucleus.

concepts.name: Pyramid
concepts.definition: An elevation on either side of the ventral median fissure of the medulla, produced by the corticospinal tract.

evidence.quote: The pyramid on each side is made by the corticospinal tract
Produced by corticospinal tract.

concepts.name: Olive
concepts.definition: An elevation on the medulla lying lateral to the pyramid, produced by the inferior olivary nucleus.

evidence.quote: the olive lateral to it by the inferior olivary nucleus
An elevation, lies lateral to the pyramid.

concepts.name: Inferior olivary nucleus
concepts.definition: The nucleus of the medulla that produces the olive; it is important in the control of movement.

evidence.quote: Olive = inferior olivary nucleus.
Produced by inferior olivary nucleus (important in control of movement).

concepts.name: Corticospinal tract
concepts.definition: A descending motor tract which, with the corticobulbar tract, forms the motor pathway for voluntary movement of the body and face. It produces the pyramid of the medulla, and 75 to 90 percent of its fibres decussate in the lower medulla.

evidence.quote: Corticospinal and corticobulbar | Descending | Voluntary movement of body and face
Pyramids = corticospinal tracts; 75-90% decussate in the lower medulla.

concepts.name: Pyramidal decussation
concepts.definition: The crossing of most corticospinal (pyramidal) fibres, 75 to 90 percent, in the lower medulla; it marks the lower part of the ventral median fissure.

evidence.quote: is marked below by the decussation of 75 to 90 percent of corticospinal fibres
Its lower part is marked by decussation of most of pyramidal(corticospinal) fibers (75%-90%).

concepts.name: Reticular formation
concepts.definition: A network of neuronal cell bodies and small axon bundles running in many directions, without distinct boundaries, spread from the spinal cord through the brainstem to the hypothalamus and thalamus. It integrates arousal, consciousness, sleep-wake cycles, motor coordination, cardiovascular and respiratory control and pain modulation.

evidence.quote: It integrates vital functions: arousal, consciousness, sleep-wake cycles, motor coordination, cardiovascular and respiratory control, pain modulation and habituation.
The reticular formation (RF) consists of an intricate mixture of neuronal cell bodies and fascicles of axons running in small bundles

concepts.name: Alternating syndrome
concepts.definition: The association of a peripheral cranial nerve palsy on one side with a hemiplegia on the opposite side. It locates the lesion to a level in the brainstem, the cranial nerve involved indicating the level.

evidence.quote: A peripheral cranial nerve lesion on one side with a hemiplegia on the other locates the lesion to a level in the brainstem.
Alternating syndrome: ipsilateral cranial nerve palsy plus contralateral hemiplegia.

concepts.name: Dorsal column-medial lemniscus pathway
concepts.definition: An ascending conscious tract running through the brainstem that carries touch, proprioception and vibration.

evidence.quote: Dorsal column-medial lemniscus | Ascending, conscious | Touch, proprioception, vibration
Conscious tracts : comprised of the dorsal column-medial lemniscal pathway and the anterolateral system.

concepts.name: Anterolateral system
concepts.definition: An ascending conscious tract running through the brainstem that carries crude touch, pain and temperature.

evidence.quote: Anterolateral (spinothalamic) | Ascending, conscious | Crude touch, pain, temperature
Conscious tracts : comprised of the dorsal column-medial lemniscal pathway and the anterolateral system.

concepts.name: Transverse fissure of Bichat
concepts.definition: The fissure at the upper limit of the brainstem, by which the brainstem connects above with the diencephalon.

evidence.quote: Above, the diencephalon by the transverse fissure of Bichat.

conflicts.issue: Slide 20 says the trochlear nerve (CN IV) innervates the 'major oblique muscle' and 'ensures upward gaze'. Standard teaching is that the trochlear nerve supplies the superior oblique muscle, which depresses (and intorts) the eye, i.e. downward gaze.

evidence.quote: Nerve IV (pathetic nerve: the only one that emerges on the posterior surface of the brainstem innervates the major oblique muscle of the eye: ensures upward gaze)

conflicts.issue: The packet lists the cephalic flexure and the mesencephalic (cranial) flexure as two separate bends, and slide 4 places the cephalic flexure between brainstem and spinal cord. In standard teaching the cephalic flexure is the mesencephalic flexure (in the midbrain region), and the bend between hindbrain and spinal cord is the cervical flexure.

evidence.quote: the cephalic flexure: brainstem and spinal cord.
The growing neural tube bends at the cephalic flexure and the mesencephalic (cranial) flexure.

conflicts.issue: The packet says the medial eminence marks the midline of the floor of the fourth ventricle (one question option calls it the 'median eminence'). In standard teaching the midline is marked by the median sulcus, with a medial eminence on each side of it; 'median eminence' is the standard name of a hypothalamic structure.

evidence.quote: The medial eminence marks the midline of the floor.
The median eminence marks the midline.

conflicts.issue: Slide 20 calls cranial nerve XI 'the spinal nerve', while slide 17 calls it the accessory nerve. The standard name is accessory nerve; 'spinal nerve' is the standard name of the nerves arising from the spinal cord, so it was not listed as an alias.

evidence.quote: XI the spinal nerve
cranial part of accessory(11th)

conflicts.issue: Slides 15 and 17 carry the heading 'DESCRIPTIVE ANATOMY: THE MIDBRAIN' but describe the floor of the fourth ventricle (pons and medulla) and the nerves emerging from the medulla; the summary places this content under the pons and medulla.

evidence.quote: DESCRIPTIVE ANATOMY: THE MIDBRAIN Posterior Surface The floor of the fourth ventricle is composed of the dorsal surface of the pons and the medulla.

notes: The packet has no known-concept list, so all names are the standard English names.

More than 50 things met the selection rules. Left out for the limit and mentioned inside other definitions where they belong: basilar groove (in Pons and Basilar artery), interpeduncular fossa (in Cerebral peduncle and Oculomotor nerve), foramina of Luschka and Magendie (in Fourth ventricle and Cerebellopontine angle), inferior quadrigeminal brachium (in Inferior colliculus), respiratory and cardiovascular centres (in Medulla oblongata), intermediate nerve of Wrisberg (in Facial nerve). Left out entirely: spinocerebellar tract (appears only as a table row and a wrong option in q:u2xf18), medial eminence, corticobulbar tract.

Acoustic neuroma at the cerebellopontine angle (hy:9, deeper:4) and trochlear nerve injury (deeper:3) are only in the high-yield and deeper blocks and are not tested by any question or flashcard, so they have no concept and no causes relation.

The packet writes 'Cerebral peduncle (crus cerebri)' in several question options; 'crus cerebri' is listed as an alias as the packet uses it, although strictly it names the anterior part of the cerebral peduncle.

Slides 3 and 5 say 'posterior cerebral fossa' / 'cerebral posterior fossa' where the summary says posterior cranial fossa; the summary wording was used and those slides were not quoted for that concept.

Slide 20 has old or translated nerve names ('common occulomotor nerve', 'external oculomotor', 'pathetic nerve', 'cochleo-vestibular', 'major oblique muscle'); correctly spelt ones were kept as aliases. Slide 17 has run-together OCR text ('sulcusdorsolateralto').
The thalamus, optic nerve and olfactory nerve are concepts because questions test them as things that are NOT brainstem; no part-of or emerges-from relation to the brainstem was written for them.
